Live-verified end-to-end on 2026-07-19: 103 real Open-Meteo weather → deterministic candidates/score/rank → **Haiku re-rank (3 named looks + one-sentence 104 "why")** → flat-lay layout → signed cutout URLs → the screen. Plan + design decisions in 119 `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-18-stylist-generator.md`. 120 121 ### The design source (authoritative) 122 `design_handoff_stylist_generator/` = a Claude Design handoff. **`README.md` + `generator-mockup-v2.html` are 123 the authoritative spec** (v2 = editorial "Lookbook" with the "Today's Looks" header + weather pill + city + 124 "Later" advice + occasion chips + Refine sheet + 01/02/03 + why-as-hero + credits). `Fitcheck.dc.html` and 125 `generator-mockup-original.html` in that folder are **byte-identical duplicates** — ignore them. 126 127 ### Review punch-list — all fixed + test-enforced 128 An adversarial review found real issues; every one is baked in as a tested decision (D1–D12 in the plan): 129 - **D1 reduced-motion**: flat-lay is `opacity:1` by default (a plain-`` path when reduced) — motion is 130 progressive enhancement. A test fails if any piece is `opacity:0` under reduce. (Fixes an invisibility bug.) 131 - **D2 contrast**: informational text ≥ `muted-foreground`; credits' **brand names are the most readable**. 132 - **D3** one look name (index === byline). **D4** occasion uses `Chip variant="select"`. **D5** the why leads 133 with the rust "f" glyph. **D6** deterministic layout templates. **D9** occasion→band model. **D10** loading/ 134 empty/error states. **D11** fragrances excluded. **D12** optional accessory slots. 135 136 --- 137 138 ## 🎯 The occasion model (reworked 2026-07-21, after PR #5) 139 140 **Occasion is CONTEXT, not a dress code.** An evening date and a black-tie dinner are both "Evening"; 141 what separates them is the user's dress code. The original narrow bands (work `[3,4.5]`, evening 142 `[3.5,5]`) baked one assumed dress code in for everyone, so a smart-casual wardrobe could not produce a 143 Work or Evening outfit **at all** — the screen just said "Add a few more pieces" with 8 items in the closet. 144 145 The resolution order is now: **occasion band → narrowed by the profile's dress codes → overridden by Refine.** 146 147 - Bands widened (`lib/generator/rules.ts`); every band includes 3 (smart casual). 148 - `personalBand()` intersects with `profiles.formality_min/max` — the answer onboarding **already 149 collected** and the generator had never selected. Padded ±0.5; falls back to the plain occasion band 150 when there's no overlap. 151 - `applyFormalityOverride` now REPLACES rather than intersects, so Refine can dress you *up* past your 152 usual ceiling (previously a smart-casual profile could never request black tie). 153 154 **Related principle — hard filters vs soft preferences.** Three filters could each silently yield zero 155 outfits from a wearable closet. Fixed: shoes get a wider formality floor (1.0 vs 0.5 — a clean sneaker is 156 valid smart-casual work wear); outerwear is no longer *required* below 15° (that gave anyone without a 157 coat nothing all winter). Empty results now name the blocking slot via `missingCategory()`. 158 159 **⚠️ The same pattern remains in `seasons`** — it's still a hard filter. The current closet's trousers are 160 tagged `{Spring,Summer,Autumn}`, so **in winter there are no eligible bottoms and every occasion returns 161 empty** (correctly explained now, but still a dead end). Either soften the seasons filter the way 162 outerwear was softened, or treat it as a tagging problem. Not yet decided. 163 164 ### Deliberate divergence from the design handoff: the occasion row 165 166 `generator-mockup-v2.html:96` specifies a scrolling chip row with a right-edge gradient fade 167 (`-webkit-mask-image`) and the Refine pill inside the row. We implemented that faithfully — and it was 168 wrong on phones. Measured with the real component: 169 170 | Shell width | Device | "Evening" visible | 171 |---|---|---| 172 | 375px | iPhone SE / 13 mini | **0%** | 173 | 390px | iPhone 14/15/16 | **0%** | 174 | 414px | Pro Max | 3% | 175 | 440px | shell cap — desktop only | 34% | 176 177 Refine cost 84px of the row (76px button + 8px gap), so on every real phone **a quarter of the feature 178 was undiscoverable** — the row read "Everyday · Work · Weekend · Refine". The 34% figure is desktop-only 179 and misled the first review; see memory `mobile-first-evaluate-at-phone-width`. 180 181 **Changed:** `OccasionRow` is now a non-scrolling `flex-1` row of four chips (13px labels), and Refine 182 moved to the header beside "Today's Looks" as `RefineButton`. Refine is a *modifier* on the chosen 183 occasion, not a fifth peer of it, so the header is also the more honest hierarchy. A scroll row suits an 184 unbounded list; four fixed options should all be reachable without a gesture. 185 186 Verified on an **iPhone 17 simulator** (Xcode is installed but `xcode-select` points at CommandLineTools — 187 use `DEVELOPER_DIR=/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents/Developer xcrun simctl …`). A test in 188 `occasion-refine.test.tsx` guards the structure (all four chips render; the row has no `overflow-x-auto` 189 or `mask-image`) so this can't silently revert. 190 191 ## ⚠️ OPEN ITEMS / next steps (in order) 192 193 1. **Merge `feat/stylist-generator` → `main`** (PR like the closet work, or direct). Commit only when the user 194 says so; **commit messages carry NO AI attribution.** 195 2. ~~**Commit the grants-fix migration**~~ **DONE** — `20260721090000_authenticated_grants.sql` is committed 196 (in `fa8176b`, alongside `20260721100000_profile_location.sql`). 197 3. ~~**Weather → real location.**~~ **DONE 2026-07-21** (8 commits on `feat/stylist-generator`, live-verified). 198 Geolocation fires **on tap** of "Use my location" in the city menu (never on load — a sticky `Block` is 199 the thing to avoid); the fix persists to `profiles.location_lat/lon/label/source/timezone/updated_at` and 200 silently refreshes on later loads when the browser already reports `granted`. **A saved city beats GPS** 201 (`location_source = 'city'` suppresses the refresh); an explicit tap still wins. **Open-Meteo needs no key.** 202 Spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-21-generator-real-location-design.md` · plan: 203 `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-21-generator-real-location.md`. 204 Three defects were fixed alongside it: 205 - **Hour labels were GMT.** No `timezone` param was sent, so the "Later" cells showed UTC — 2h off in 206 Berlin. Now `&timezone=auto`, and `mapForecast` derives its now-index from `raw.current.time` (local at 207 the location) instead of a UTC `nowIso`. Verified live across zones: Tokyo shows Tokyo's hours. 208 - **The forecast cache could never hit.** `fetchForecast` caches per URL (`revalidate: 1800`), but raw GPS 209 precision makes every URL unique. Coords are now rounded to 2dp (~1.1km) at the fetch boundary and 210 before persisting — also less precise personal data stored. 211 - **A chosen city was clobbered** by the silent refresh on every load (race + the stored `location_source` 212 never being read back). Fixed in `ca3c1bd`; see decision L8 in the spec. 213 4. **Re-onboard to re-test** — local DB was reset this session, so all local data (user + items) is wiped. Sign 214 in (email magic-link via Mailpit `http://127.0.0.1:54324`) → quiz → capture a few items → `/generate`. 215 Note: an oxford at formality 4 won't fit "Everyday" [1.5,3]; tag it 3 for a valid Everyday combo. 216 5. **Roadmap (Plans 07–13):** outfit detail · Style DNA · OOTD calendar/diary · saved outfits · profile hub · 217 wear stats · share cards. Scoped in `docs/prototype-review.md`. 218 219 Smaller polish: eyeball reduced-motion live; show accessories in the flat-lay; fragrance "finishing-touch" line; 220 free-text occasion intent (Plan-06 addition C — currently Refine = formality + palette only). 221 222 --- 223 224 ## 🐛 DB gotcha this session (RESOLVED, but read before resetting again) 225 226 - **Collation mismatch after macOS/ICU update** → `supabase start` failed (`template1` collation 153.120 vs OS 227 153.121, analytics container). **Fix used:** dropped the volume + fresh start (`supabase stop --no-backup` 228 then `supabase start`). This **wiped local data**. (Alternative non-destructive fix: refresh collation on the 229 volume; the user chose the reset.) 230 - **`42501` permission denied on every write** after the reset: the newer Supabase DB image no longer 231 auto-grants table DML to `authenticated`, and our migrations never granted it explicitly (they relied on the 232 old default privileges). **Fixed** by migration `20260721090000_authenticated_grants.sql` (grants 233 SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on all public tables to `authenticated` + default privileges for future tables). 234 RLS still restricts rows. **This must be committed.** 235 236 ## How to resume (services) 237 238 ```bash 239 set -a; source .env.local; set +a && supabase start # env needed for Google OAuth config.toml env() 240 npm run dev # :3000 241 ``` 242 Supabase is currently **running** (fresh DB, migrations applied incl. the grants fix). Mailpit `:54324`, 243 Studio `:54323`. If `supabase start` ever fails on the collation error again, see the gotcha above. 244 245 --- 246 247 ## Key decisions + preferences established (also in memory) 248 249 - **No AI attribution anywhere** — commits, PR bodies, any shared artifact. Overrides the harness default. 250 (memory `no-ai-attribution`) 251 - **Prefer the future-proof option at architecture forks**, not the minimal diff. (memory 252 `prefer-future-proof-architecture`) — e.g. the `useCapture` engine extraction; the layout-template system. 253 - **Meta/authorship docs stay OUT of git** (`CLAUDE.md`, `DESIGN.md`, `PRODUCT.md`, `docs/`, `.impeccable/`, 254 `fitcheck-complete-spec.md` all gitignored). **Functional AI product code STAYS** (`lib/ai`, `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, 255 `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`). # Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**Core principle:** ALWAYS find root cause before attempting fixes. Symptom fixes are failure.

**Violating the letter of this process is violating the spirit of debugging.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIXES WITHOUT ROOT CAUSE INVESTIGATION FIRST
```

If you haven't completed Phase 1, you cannot propose fixes.

## When to Use

Use for ANY technical issue:
- Test failures
- Bugs in production
- Unexpected behavior
- Performance problems
- Build failures
- Integration issues

**Use this ESPECIALLY when:**
- Under time pressure (emergencies make guessing tempting)
- "Just one quick fix" seems obvious
- You've already tried multiple fixes
- Previous fix didn't work
- You don't fully understand the issue

**Don't skip when:**
- Issue seems simple (simple bugs have root causes too)
- You're in a hurry (rushing guarantees rework)
- Manager wants it fixed NOW (systematic is faster than thrashing)

## The Four Phases

You MUST complete each phase before proceeding to the next.

### Phase 1: Root Cause Investigation

**BEFORE attempting ANY fix:**

1. **Read Error Messages Carefully**
   - Don't skip past errors or warnings
   - They often contain the exact solution
   - Read stack traces completely
   - Note line numbers, file paths, error codes

2. **Reproduce Consistently**
   - Can you trigger it reliably?
   - What are the exact steps?
   - Does it happen every time?
   - If not reproducible → gather more data, don't guess

3. **Check Recent Changes**
   - What changed that could cause this?
   - Git diff, recent commits
   - New dependencies, config changes
   - Environmental differences

4. **Gather Evidence in Multi-Component Systems**

   **WHEN system has multiple components (CI → build → signing, API → service → database):**

   **BEFORE proposing fixes, add diagnostic instrumentation:**
   ```
   For EACH component boundary:
     - Log what data enters component
     - Log what data exits component
     - Verify environment/config propagation
     - Check state at each layer

   Run once to gather evidence showing WHERE it breaks
   THEN analyze evidence to identify failing component
   THEN investigate that specific component
   ```

   **Example (multi-layer system):**
   ```bash
   # Layer 1: Workflow
   echo "=== Secrets available in workflow: ==="
   echo "IDENTITY: ${IDENTITY:+SET}${IDENTITY:-UNSET}"

   # Layer 2: Build script
   echo "=== Env vars in build script: ==="
   env | grep IDENTITY || echo "IDENTITY not in environment"

   # Layer 3: Signing script
   echo "=== Keychain state: ==="
   security list-keychains
   security find-identity -v

   # Layer 4: Actual signing
   codesign --sign "$IDENTITY" --verbose=4 "$APP"
   ```

   **This reveals:** Which layer fails (secrets → workflow ✓, workflow → build ✗)

5. **Trace Data Flow**

   **WHEN error is deep in call stack:**

   See `root-cause-tracing.md` in this directory for the complete backward tracing technique.

   **Quick version:**
   - Where does bad value originate?
   - What called this with bad value?
   - Keep tracing up until you find the source
   - Fix at source, not at symptom

### Phase 2: Pattern Analysis

**Find the pattern before fixing:**

1. **Find Working Examples**
   - Locate similar working code in same codebase
   - What works that's similar to what's broken?

2. **Compare Against References**
   - If implementing pattern, read reference implementation COMPLETELY
   - Don't skim - read every line
   - Understand the pattern fully before applying

3. **Identify Differences**
   - What's different between working and broken?
   - List every difference, however small
   - Don't assume "that can't matter"

4. **Understand Dependencies**
   - What other components does this need?
   - What settings, config, environment?
   - What assumptions does it make?

### Phase 3: Hypothesis and Testing

**Scientific method:**

1. **Form Single Hypothesis**
   - State clearly: "I think X is the root cause because Y"
   - Write it down
   - Be specific, not vague

2. **Test Minimally**
   - Make the SMALLEST possible change to test hypothesis
   - One variable at a time
   - Don't fix multiple things at once

3. **Verify Before Continuing**
   - Did it work? Yes → Phase 4
   - Didn't work? Form NEW hypothesis
   - DON'T add more fixes on top

4. **When You Don't Know**
   - Say "I don't understand X"
   - Don't pretend to know
   - Ask for help
   - Research more

### Phase 4: Implementation

**Fix the root cause, not the symptom:**

1. **Create Failing Test Case**
   - Simplest possible reproduction
   - Automated test if possible
   - One-off test script if no framework
   - MUST have before fixing
   - Use the `superpowers:test-driven-development` skill for writing proper failing tests

2. **Implement Single Fix**
   - Address the root cause identified
   - ONE change at a time
   - No "while I'm here" improvements
   - No bundled refactoring

3. **Verify Fix**
   - Test passes now?
   - No other tests broken?
   - Issue actually resolved?
   - Use the `superpowers:verification-before-completion` skill before claiming success

4. **If Fix Doesn't Work**
   - STOP
   - Count: How many fixes have you tried?
   - If < 3: Return to Phase 1, re-analyze with new information
   - **If ≥ 3: STOP and question the architecture (step 5 below)**
   - DON'T attempt Fix #4 without architectural discussion

5. **If 3+ Fixes Failed: Question Architecture**

   **Pattern indicating architectural problem:**
   - Each fix reveals new shared state/coupling/problem in different place
   - Fixes require "massive refactoring" to implement
   - Each fix creates new symptoms elsewhere

   **STOP and question fundamentals:**
   - Is this pattern fundamentally sound?
   - Are we "sticking with it through sheer inertia"?
   - Should we refactor architecture vs. continue fixing symptoms?

   **Discuss with your human partner before attempting more fixes**

   This is NOT a failed hypothesis - this is a wrong architecture.

## Red Flags - STOP and Follow Process

If you catch yourself thinking:
- "Quick fix for now, investigate later"
- "Just try changing X and see if it works"
- "Add multiple changes, run tests"
- "Skip the test, I'll manually verify"
- "It's probably X, let me fix that"
- "I don't fully understand but this might work"
- "Pattern says X but I'll adapt it differently"
- "Here are the main problems: [lists fixes without investigation]"
- Proposing solutions before tracing data flow
- **"One more fix attempt" (when already tried 2+)**
- **Each fix reveals new problem in different place**

**ALL of these mean: STOP. Return to Phase 1.**

**If 3+ fixes failed:** Question the architecture (see Phase 4.5)

## your human partner's Signals You're Doing It Wrong

**Watch for these redirections:**
- "Is that not happening?" - You assumed without verifying
- "Will it show us...?" - You should have added evidence gathering
- "Stop guessing" - You're proposing fixes without understanding
- "Ultra-think this" - Question fundamentals, not just symptoms
- "We're stuck?" (frustrated) - Your approach isn't working

**When you see these:** STOP. Return to Phase 1.

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Issue is simple, don't need process" | Simple issues have root causes too. Process is fast for simple bugs. |
| "Emergency, no time for process" | Systematic debugging is FASTER than guess-and-check thrashing. |
| "Just try this first, then investigate" | First fix sets the pattern. Do it right from the start. |
| "I'll write test after confirming fix works" | Untested fixes don't stick. Test first proves it. |
| "Multiple fixes at once saves time" | Can't isolate what worked. Causes new bugs. |
| "Reference too long, I'll adapt the pattern" | Partial understanding guarantees bugs. Read it completely. |
| "I see the problem, let me fix it" | Seeing symptoms ≠ understanding root cause. |
| "One more fix attempt" (after 2+ failures) | 3+ failures = architectural problem. Question pattern, don't fix again. |

## Quick Reference

| Phase | Key Activities | Success Criteria |
|-------|---------------|------------------|
| **1. Root Cause** | Read errors, reproduce, check changes, gather evidence | Understand WHAT and WHY |
| **2. Pattern** | Find working examples, compare | Identify differences |
| **3. Hypothesis** | Form theory, test minimally | Confirmed or new hypothesis |
| **4. Implementation** | Create test, fix, verify | Bug resolved, tests pass |

## When Process Reveals "No Root Cause"

If systematic investigation reveals issue is truly environmental, timing-dependent, or external:

1. You've completed the process
2. Document what you investigated
3. Implement appropriate handling (retry, timeout, error message)
4. Add monitoring/logging for future investigation

**But:** 95% of "no root cause" cases are incomplete investigation.

## Supporting Techniques

These techniques are part of systematic debugging and available in this directory:

- **`root-cause-tracing.md`** - Trace bugs backward through call stack to find original trigger
- **`defense-in-depth.md`** - Add validation at multiple layers after finding root cause
- **`condition-based-waiting.md`** - Replace arbitrary timeouts with condition polling

I have a measured root cause, and it isn't quite what the audit plan predicted. Evidence:

**On your real closet (11 tops, 6 bottoms, 3 shoes), Everyday/Summer produces 48 valid combos — and the re-ranker is handed 6 of them. In winter it's handed exactly 3.**

The model is asked to "pick the best 3." In winter it's picking 3 from 3 — regenerate is *mathematically incapable* of returning anything different. In summer it picks 3 from 6, so it lands on near-identical sets.

The chain:

- `app/generate/actions.ts:134` passes `excludeItemIds: []` on every call, regenerates included — so the input is identical. My probe confirms `buildCandidates → rankTopN → diversify` is byte-identical across consecutive runs (`identical: true`). That's **S1**, as predicted.
- But the bigger factor is `lib/generator/diversity.ts:60-71`. `diversify` only keeps a combo when **both** its top and bottom are unused, then **backfills only to a floor of 3, never to `n`**. With 6 bottoms, at most 6 combos can ever pass. The other 42 — which is where all the shoe variation lives — are discarded, not offered as secondary variety.

That second part came from `2e88d39` ("never pad the shortlist with repeats"), which is on the branch I just told you to merge. The commit is right about not padding with duplicates; what wasn't costed is that it also shrinks the model's choice set from 20 to `min(distinct tops, distinct bottoms)`. Those are two different things — the *final three* must be distinct, but the *shortlist* wants to be large.

Decisive: **in winter, excluding the previous set's tops+bottoms leaves 0 combos** — a naive exclusion would turn Regenerate into "Nothing to style yet." (Your closet has only 3 winter-tagged bottoms; excluding 3 removes them all.)

Full picture:

| | 1st gen | after excluding prev. tops+bottoms |
|---|---|---|
| Everyday / Summer | 48 combos → 6 shortlist | 15 combos → 3 shortlist |
| Everyday / Winter | 21 combos → **3** shortlist | **0 combos** |
| Work / Winter | 24 combos → **3** shortlist | **0 combos** |

So the fix is two parts, and part 1 is the prerequisite:

1. **Stop the shortlist collapsing.** `diversify` should still put maximally-distinct combos *first* (so the model's best-3 stay distinct by construction), but then fill to `n` in tiers of decreasing strictness rather than truncating at 3. Today 42 of 48 valid combos — everything with shoe variation — are thrown away.
2. **Wire `excludeItemIds` on regenerate**, with a fallback for exactly the winter case above.

One decision I shouldn't make for you, since it changes what Regenerate *means*:

content.text:
Confirmed the seam exists. Here's my honest read.

**All four options I gave you were hard filters** — they remove items from the closet before candidates are built. Your project has already learned this lesson twice, and it's written down in `docs/STATE.md` as a named principle: *hard filters vs soft preferences*. Three filters could each silently yield zero outfits from a wearable closet; outerwear-below-15° and the shoes formality floor were both softened for exactly that reason. The seasons filter is the known third case still outstanding — it's queue plan #1.

A hard `excludeItemIds` on regenerate would be the fourth instance of the same mistake. My own measurement already caught it doing so: 0 combos in winter. The "fallback" I attached to each option is the tell — I was designing an escape hatch for a mechanism that shouldn't be able to fail that way.

**What fits the project goal better: make "recently shown" a soft preference, not a filter.**

`rankTopN` takes a `Ctx` that already carries `lean` — the Refine colour preference, which reorders the shortlist toward requested families and is *dropped silently when the closet can't honour it*. That is precisely the semantics regenerate wants. Adding `recentlyShown: string[]` as a scoring penalty means:

- Previously-shown pieces sink in the ranking instead of vanishing from the closet.
- It **cannot** return empty. On a 5-item closet straight out of onboarding — where there may be exactly one valid combo — you get that combo back with an honest "this is the best I have," not "Nothing to style yet."
- It stays deterministic and unit-testable, which was a deliberate property of this pipeline.
- It composes with the seasons work in plan #1 rather than fighting it.

`excludeItemIds` stays where it is, unused, for a case that genuinely is hard — items away at the cleaners, or packed for a trip.

**Sequencing.** Two independent changes, and I'd ship them separately:

1. **Fix the shortlist collapse** (`diversify` fills to `n` in tiers instead of truncating at 3). This is a defect on its own terms — 42 of 48 combos discarded means your *daily* looks never vary by shoes either, not just your regenerated ones. It ships and gets measured alone.
2. **Then re-measure regenerate.** With 20 real candidates instead of 3, Haiku's own sampling may already produce a visibly different set. If it does, part 2 is unnecessary and regenerate keeps its promise for free. If it doesn't, add the `recentlyShown` penalty on that evidence.

I'd genuinely rather measure step 1's effect than assume it. There's also a monetisation argument for getting this right: queue #8 turns regenerate into the Pro gate (3/day free, unlimited Pro), so it needs to visibly deliver before it's metered.

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write comprehensive implementation plans assuming the engineer has zero context for our codebase and questionable taste. Document everything they need to know: which files to touch for each task, code, testing, docs they might need to check, how to test it. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

Assume they are a skilled developer, but know almost nothing about our toolset or problem domain. Assume they don't know good test design very well.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Bite-Sized Task Granularity

**Each step is one action (2-5 minutes):**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Write minimal implementation**

```python
def function(input):
    return expected
```

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## No Placeholders

Every step must contain the actual content an engineer needs. These are **plan failures** — never write them:
- "TBD", "TODO", "implement later", "fill in details"
- "Add appropriate error handling" / "add validation" / "handle edge cases"
- "Write tests for the above" (without actual test code)
- "Similar to Task N" (repeat the code — the engineer may be reading tasks out of order)
- Steps that describe what to do without showing how (code blocks required for code steps)
- References to types, functions, or methods not defined in any task

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Placeholder scan:** Search your plan for red flags — any of the patterns from the "No Placeholders" section above. Fix them.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving the plan, offer execution choice:

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Two execution options:**

**1. Subagent-Driven (recommended)** - I dispatch a fresh subagent per task, review between tasks, fast iteration

**2. Inline Execution** - Execute tasks in this session using executing-plans, batch execution with checkpoints

**Which approach?"**

**If Subagent-Driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development
- Fresh subagent per task + two-stage review

**If Inline Execution chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
- Batch execution with checkpoints for review

content.text:
Confirmed, and it's a **pre-existing bug at the magic moment**, not something my changes introduced:

- The JSON schema sent to the API has **no** `minItems`/`maxItems` — `forStructuredOutput` strips them (exactly as CLAUDE.md documents). The model is free to return any number of picks.
- `RerankSchema.parse` then demands *exactly* 3 (`.length(3)`) and **throws** on fewer.

So any closet with fewer than 3 viable candidates errors out. That includes a closet straight out of onboarding's "capture your first five" — the magic moment CLAUDE.md says must never be gated. `rerank.ts:26-34` already warns about this exact failure for names ("a hard bound here existed only as a post-hoc throw that failed the ENTIRE generation and surfaced as 'Couldn't reach the stylist'. Repair, don't reject") — the array length was missed.

It's the acceptance criterion of my own plan's Step 7, so I'm fixing it, test-first, as a clearly separate commit:

input.command:
gh pr create --base main --head fix/regenerate-variety --title "fix(gen): make Regenerate return a different set" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
Regenerate returned the same looks every time. Root-caused by measurement before any code changed.

## What was actually wrong

Two causes, the second larger than expected.

**1. The shortlist collapsed.** `diversify` only kept a combo when *both* its top and bottom were unused, then backfilled to a floor of 3 — so at most `min(distinct tops, distinct bottoms)` combos survived. Measured on a real 21-item closet (11 tops / 6 bottoms / 3 shoes):

| Occasion / season | valid combos | handed to the re-ranker |
|---|---|---|
| Everyday / Summer | 48 | **6** |
| Work / Summer | 48 | **6** |
| Everyday / Winter | 21 | **3** |
| Work / Winter | 24 | **3** |

In winter the model picked 3 from 3 — Regenerate was mathematically incapable of returning anything else. All shoe variation lived in the 42 discarded combos.

**2. The input was identical between runs.** `buildCandidates → rankTopN → diversify` is fully deterministic, and `actions.ts` passed `excludeItemIds: []` on every call, regenerates included.

## The fix

**Tiered shortlist.** Combos with a fresh top *and* bottom come first, then those with one fresh slot, then the rest — score-ordered within each tier, filled to `n`. The model still sees maximally-distinct options at the head, so its best-3 stay distinct, but the tail is no longer thrown away. Same closet now yields a 20-candidate shortlist in every season.

This reverses part of `2e88d39` ("never pad the shortlist with repeats"). That commit was right that padding with *duplicates* is bad, and wrong that a combo sharing one slot is a duplicate: three looks sharing trousers but differing in top and shoes are three different looks, and `buildCandidates` never emits the same combination twice.

**A soft `recentlyShown` preference, not a hard filter.** On a regenerate, the replaced set's item ids are fed into ranking as a proportional score penalty (`RECENT_WEIGHT = 0.25`), so just-shown pieces sink but are never removed from the closet.

A hard `excludeItemIds` filter was measured and rejected: excluding the previous set's tops+bottoms yields **0 combos in winter** on this closet, turning Regenerate into "Nothing to style yet". That is the same hard-filter trap already fixed for outerwear and the shoes formality floor. `excludeItemIds` stays unused, reserved for a genuinely hard exclusion later.

## A pre-existing bug found while verifying

Verifying the small-closet safety property surfaced a separate defect: `RerankSchema` demanded *exactly* 3 picks, but `forStructuredOutput` strips `minItems`/`maxItems`, so the count was never enforced on the model — it existed only as a post-hoc throw. Any closet with fewer than three viable combos failed the whole generation as "Couldn't reach the stylist", including one straight out of onboarding's "capture your first five". Now `.min(1)` with the cap applied in `finalisePicks`. Same "repair, don't reject" stance the file already applies to overlong names.

## Verification

- 228 tests green, `tsc` clean, `npm run build` clean.
- Live on an iPhone 17 simulator and in the browser: two consecutive regenerates returned three different looks, with three *different pairs of shoes* where all three previously shared one.
- Small-closet safety: reduced to a single viable combo, Regenerate returns that look again with a fresh "why" — not an error, not an empty screen. Before the rerank fix the same closet showed "Couldn't reach the stylist".

Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/todo/2026-07-28-regenerate-variety.md` (gitignored).
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -2

content.text:
## The problem

`lib/generator/candidates.ts:44` — one line:

```ts
if (i.seasons.length && !i.seasons.includes(a.season)) return false;
```

A season tag **eliminates** an item rather than deprioritising it. It's the third instance of the hard-filter trap this project has already fixed twice (outerwear below 15°, the shoes formality floor) — and the only one still live.

On your closet right now: 3 of 6 bottoms and **your only coat** are not tagged Winter. So in winter the generator has one-third fewer trousers and no outerwear whatsoever. It's also why the winter numbers in yesterday's investigation were so small — 21 valid combos vs 48 in summer.

The failure mode is worse than "fewer options": a single mis-tagged slot zeroes the whole screen. If your three winter-tagged bottoms happened to fall outside the formality band, every occasion would return "Add a few more pieces" with a perfectly wearable closet. AI tagging produced these tags, and it's ~90% right — so this *will* happen to real users.

## Yes, there's a plan — and it's queue #1

`docs/superpowers/plans/todo/2026-07-24-seasons-soft-preference.md`, 6 tasks. The approach matches what we just did for regenerate:

- Season logic moves into `lib/generator/season.ts`
- The hard filter in `isEligible` is **deleted**
- `buildCandidates` orders each category **in-season-first**, so the 200-combo cap can't discard the good ones
- `scoreCombo` gains a weighted `seasonFit` term, so in-season combos rank above off-season ones
- Measured weather (temperature, rain) **keeps** filtering hard — that's a real reading, not a coarse month label

That last distinction is the right one: a thermometer saying 2°C is evidence; a `{Spring, Summer}` tag on trousers is a guess.

## Two defects I just fixed in the plan

The plan predates today's work and would have silently reverted it:

1. It pasted a full `Ctx` type without `recentlyShown` — applying it verbatim deletes the regenerate signal. (`tsc` would have caught it, but the tempting "fix" is to delete the feature.)
2. Its `rankTopN` call site read `rankTopN(combos, {...}, 20)`. The current code ranks *all* combos then calls `diversify(ranked, 20)`. The "change from" text no longer exists in the file, and forcing it would drop `diversify` entirely — reintroducing both bugs from PR #14 and #15.

I corrected both and added a warning note against re-collapsing the call. Worth flagging that the 2026-07-27 review pass caught this same plan pasting a pre-fix `buildCandidates` — it's now bitten twice, so it's worth re-reading its code snippets against live code before executing rather than trusting them.

Checked your system before answering. You have an **authored** design: Libre Caslon Text + Hanken Grotesk, "stylist's studio after dark… quiet luxury in the register of SSENSE and Mr Porter," and `DESIGN.md` explicitly uses gradients.

That's the deciding factor. These skills split into three groups, and only one is safe to point at the app.

## Worth using

**`imagegen-frontend-mobile`** — the strongest fit, and useful *now*, not at the end. Your three scoping docs are blocked on design decisions for screens that have no design at all: packing mode ("a Pro feature the design names and specifies nowhere"), stylist chat, "See curated picks", and the wear-stats gap analysis. This generates mobile screen concepts in phone mockups and touches no code — exactly what unblocks those conversations. It's also the only one here that's mobile-native rather than web-first.

**`redesign-existing-projects`** — the best match for the #16 audit, better than `design-taste-frontend`. It's audit-first, explicitly hunts "generic AI patterns", and says "without breaking functionality". Use its audit half; ignore its style prescriptions wherever they meet Midnight Atelier.

## Later, for things that don't exist yet

**`brandkit`** — your `public/` still ships `next.svg` and `vercel.svg`. PWA icons, app-store assets and a brand board are genuinely unbuilt, and this is built for that. Not product UI though.

**`imagegen-frontend-web`** — for the marketing site at launch and the Phase-2 `@vercel/og` share cards. Nothing to do with the app itself.

## Don't point these at Fitcheck

**`minimalist-ui`** — says "no gradients, no heavy shadows". `DESIGN.md` uses gradients, and queue item #2 (`design-tokens`) is literally *"cream ramp, surface gradients, hairline scale"*. It would fight the plan you're about to execute.

**`high-end-visual-design`** — "defines the exact fonts, spacing, shadows." You already chose Libre Caslon Text and Hanken Grotesk deliberately. A second opinionated font stack is drift, and drift is the exact problem `docs/design-review-2026-07-24.md` already catalogues.

**`industrial-brutalist-ui`** — military terminal and declassified blueprints, versus a stylist's studio after dark. Straight opposite.

**`full-output-enforcement`** — not a design skill at all.

## The general rule

Skills that **generate** options where you have nothing (imagegen-mobile, brandkit) are safe. Skills that **audit against your system** (impeccable, redesign-existing-projects) are useful. Skills that **impose their own taste** (high-end-visual-design, minimalist-ui, industrial-brutalist) are a liability *because* you already have a design authored and documented — they don't know about Midnight Atelier and will quietly overwrite it.

Want me to add `imagegen-frontend-mobile` to the scoping docs as the way to unblock those four undesigned screens? That's the one with value today rather than fifteen plans out.

146	 * of an opinion, not a reason to rank it last.
147	 */
148	export function inSeason(seasons: string[] | undefined, season: string | undefined): boolean {

150	  if (!seasons || seasons.length === 0) return true;

152	  return seasons.some((x) => x.toLowerCase() === s);

The last hard filter in the generator. A season tag could silently zero a wearable closet; it now orders and scores candidates, the same soft-preference model already used for outerwear and the Refine colour lean.

## The defect, measured

A season tag ran against every **required** slot, so one narrowly-tagged category zeroed everything. On a constructed closet — 10 tops, 4 bottoms, 4 shoes, every piece wearable, the trousers simply lacking a Winter tag:

| | combos |
|---|---|
| Summer | 40 |
| Winter | **0** — `missingCategory` blames Bottoms |

On the real 21-item development closet there were **no** dead ends (the earlier claim in `docs/STATE.md` was out of date — it has 3 winter-tagged bottoms), but the cost was still heavy:

| occasion | winter combos, before → after |
|---|---|
| Everyday | 21 → **60** |
| Work | 24 → **60** |
| Weekend | 24 → **66** |
| Evening | 24 → **60** |

Its single coat is tagged `{Spring, Autumn}`, so **winter previously had no outerwear at all**. It now has it in every season.

## The change

- `lib/generator/season.ts` — new. `inSeason`, `seasonFit`, `currentSeason`. Case-insensitive, because the DB stores Title case and the fixtures use lower.
- The hard filter is gone from `isEligible`. Season now does two soft things instead: `eligibleByCategory` orders each category **in-season-first** (so the 200-combo cap can't discard the good ones), and `scoreCombo` gains a weighted `seasonFit` term (`SEASON_WEIGHT = 0.2`). An off-season combo still scores above zero, so it is always offered rather than the screen going empty.

## The protection it replaces

Deleting the filter also deletes the only thing keeping a wool sweater out of a July outfit — so it is **replaced with the measured equivalent**, not simply removed. `weatherRules` gains heat-based material exclusions above 25°C, driven by the temperature we already fetch. A coarse month-derived label is swapped for a real reading of the day, which is the whole argument.

Verified live at **29°C** on the development closet: the wool trousers are eligible at 20° and excluded at 29°.

## A pre-existing dead end fixed alongside

`excludeMaterials` was itself a hard filter, so a closet whose only shoes were suede already returned zero outfits in the rain. Adding a heat list would have multiplied that risk, so one rule now covers both: **a weather exclusion may narrow a required slot but may never empty it.** If it would, that slot is refilled without the exclusion. Relief is scoped to weather — a formality gap is a real wardrobe gap and is still reported by `missingCategory`.

Material matching also moved from equality to **substring**. The tagger writes free text, so `"suede leather"` already slipped past the rain rule and `"merino wool"` would have slipped past the heat rule.

## Verification

- 254 tests green, `tsc` clean, `npm run build` clean.
- `coverage.test.ts` and `shortlist-size.test.ts` — the guards for PR #14 and #15 — run explicitly after every task touching `candidates.ts`. The combo-generation loop was not modified; only how the five category lists feeding it are derived.
- Live on an iPhone 17 simulator: three looks generate correctly at 29°C, no wool in any of them.

## Known trade-off

With a thin closet you can now get a mildly off-season piece, because ranking prefers rather than forbids. Deliberate, and consistent with `personalBand`'s existing stance — better a slightly-off outfit than none.

You're right, and the data proves it's worse than a theoretical objection.

`lib/ai/tagging-schema.ts:10` is `material: z.string().min(1)` — free text, no weight, no weave, no enum. And the real values are single words: `Wool`, `Cotton`, `Linen`, `knit`, `Polyester, Viscose`.

So the field cannot distinguish tropical/fresco/high-twist wool — which is *excellent* hot-weather tailoring — from melton, flannel or boiled wool. Merino is the sharpest case: it's used for summer base layers precisely because it wicks and breathes, and my substring match excludes `"merino wool"` outright. That's backwards.

The bug is that I excluded on **fiber**, when heat is decided by **weight and weave**. Fiber is the one attribute we have and the one that doesn't answer the question.

What I'd change: keep hard exclusions only for constructions that are unambiguously cold-weather — those terms *are* weight/weave, so they're honest — and let bare `Wool` fall through to the soft signal. It isn't unprotected: a wool sweater tagged `{Autumn, Winter}` still takes the `seasonFit` penalty and ranks below a linen shirt in July. It just isn't eliminated on a guess.

**What's best:** narrow the hard exclusion to fabrics that are hot *regardless of construction*, and let ranking carry the rest.

- **Drop `wool`** — weight and weave decide, exactly as you said. Tropical, fresco and high-twist are summer suiting.
- **Drop `merino wool`** — worst offender. Merino is used *for* heat; excluding it is backwards.
- **Drop `cashmere`** — mostly cold-weather, but fine-gauge exists. Ranking, not veto.
- **Drop `corduroy`** — it's cotton, mid-season at worst.
- **Keep `fleece`, `down`, `shearling`, `quilted`, `puffer`** — these are *insulation*; no weave makes them summer-appropriate.
- **Keep `tweed`** — that one genuinely is a weave, and it's coarse heavy woolen by definition.

Nothing goes unprotected: a wool sweater tagged `{Autumn, Winter}` still takes the `seasonFit` penalty and ranks below linen in July. It's demoted on evidence rather than eliminated on a guess — which is the same argument this whole PR makes about season.

The last hard filter in the generator. A season tag could silently zero a wearable closet; it now orders and scores candidates, the same soft-preference model already used for outerwear and the Refine colour lean.

## The defect, measured

A season tag ran against every **required** slot, so one narrowly-tagged category zeroed everything. On a constructed closet — 10 tops, 4 bottoms, 4 shoes, every piece wearable, the trousers simply lacking a Winter tag:

| | combos |
|---|---|
| Summer | 40 |
| Winter | **0** — `missingCategory` blames Bottoms |

On the real 21-item development closet there were **no** dead ends (the earlier claim in `docs/STATE.md` was out of date — it has 3 winter-tagged bottoms), but the cost was still heavy:

| occasion | winter combos, before → after |
|---|---|
| Everyday | 21 → **60** |
| Work | 24 → **60** |
| Weekend | 24 → **66** |
| Evening | 24 → **60** |

Its single coat is tagged `{Spring, Autumn}`, so **winter previously had no outerwear at all**. It now has it in every season.

## The change

- `lib/generator/season.ts` — new. `inSeason`, `seasonFit`, `currentSeason`. Case-insensitive, because the DB stores Title case and the fixtures use lower.
- The hard filter is gone from `isEligible`. Season now does two soft things instead: `eligibleByCategory` orders each category **in-season-first** (so the 200-combo cap can't discard the good ones), and `scoreCombo` gains a weighted `seasonFit` term (`SEASON_WEIGHT = 0.2`). An off-season combo still scores above zero, so it is always offered rather than the screen going empty.

## The protection it replaces — and what it deliberately does not claim

Deleting the filter also deletes the only thing keeping a fleece out of a July outfit, so it is replaced with a measured equivalent: `weatherRules` gains material exclusions above 25°C, driven by the temperature we already fetch.

That list is deliberately short, and **does not contain wool**. Whether a wool garment suits 30°C is decided by its weight and weave, not its fibre — tropical, fresco and high-twist wools are summer suiting, and merino is worn *for* heat because it wicks. `items.material` is a bare fibre name (`Wool`, `Cotton`, `Linen`), so a "wool" rule cannot tell a summer-weight trouser from a melton coat; it would bin exactly the smart-casual work wear this app exists to style. What remains — fleece, down, shearling, quilted, puffer, tweed — is insulation or a coarse heavy weave, where no construction makes it summer-appropriate.

Wool is not unprotected: an off-season piece still takes the `seasonFit` penalty and ranks below linen in July. Demoted on evidence rather than eliminated on a guess — the same argument this PR makes about season.

The real fix is data. `item-data-completeness` (queue #3) adds `items.texture` (Flat / Fine knit / Chunky knit / Brushed / Fleece-back) and splits `Wool` from `Merino wool` in a constrained vocabulary; `item-signals-in-generator` (queue #12) feeds material × texture into **scoring**. Warmth belongs there as a weighted signal, not here as a veto.

## A pre-existing dead end fixed alongside

`excludeMaterials` was itself a hard filter, so a closet whose only shoes were suede already returned zero outfits in the rain. Adding a heat list would have multiplied that risk, so one rule now covers both: **a weather exclusion may narrow a required slot but may never empty it.** If it would, that slot is refilled without the exclusion. Relief is scoped to weather — a formality gap is a real wardrobe gap and is still reported by `missingCategory`.

Material matching also moved from equality to **substring**. The tagger writes free text, so `"suede leather"` already slipped past the rain rule and `"polar fleece"` would have slipped past the heat rule.

## Verification

- 256 tests green, `tsc` clean, `npm run build` clean.
- `coverage.test.ts` and `shortlist-size.test.ts` — the guards for PR #14 and #15 — run explicitly after every task touching `candidates.ts`. The combo-generation loop was not modified; only how the five category lists feeding it are derived.
- Live on an iPhone 17 simulator at a real 29°C: three looks generate correctly, and a `tropical wool` trouser is confirmed still eligible at 32°C while `polar fleece` is excluded.

## Known trade-off

With a thin closet you can now get a mildly off-season piece, because ranking prefers rather than forbids. Deliberate, and consistent with `personalBand`'s existing stance — better a slightly-off outfit than none.

Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/todo/2026-07-24-seasons-soft-preference.md` (gitignored).
EOF

Checked. Short answer: **no, and two of the gaps are real bugs** — including one I just introduced.

**`TEXTURES` has no `"Other"`.** `MATERIALS` ends with `"Other"` and the prompt says *"use Other only if none fit"* — but `texture: z.enum(TEXTURES)` is required with no escape hatch. A structured-output call forces the model to pick one of 12, so an unfamiliar fabric gets a confident wrong answer instead of an honest one.

**My heat rule will silently stop working after #3.** `HOT_MATERIALS` is `fleece, shearling, down, quilted, puffer, tweed`. Against the constrained vocabulary: `fleece` ✓, `down` ✓, `tweed` ✓ — but `shearling` and `puffer` aren't in `MATERIALS` at all, and `quilted` is a **texture**, not a material. Three of six stop matching the moment `material` becomes an enum. Today it works only because the column is free text.

Missing from `MATERIALS` that would change a styling decision: **Acrylic** (arguably the most common high-street knitwear fibre — and this closet is Zara and Massimo Dutti), **Shearling**, **Faux leather** (behaves differently from leather in rain), **Modal**. Missing heat-relevant textures: **Mesh / open knit**, **Terry**, **Seersucker** — all of which decide whether something is summer-wearable.

**Blends can't be expressed.** `material: z.enum(MATERIALS)` is single-select, and your DB already contains `"Polyester, Viscose"`. The plan's own test shows `normalizeMaterial("merino wool blend") → "Merino wool"`, so blends get flattened to their dominant fibre. Probably the right call, but it should be a stated decision rather than a side effect.

**On the underlying question though** — I don't think exhaustiveness is the goal, and it works against "simplify user input" in two ways:

1. **The user doesn't type these; the AI writes them and the user corrects.** So the list should match what a model can reliably judge *from a photo*. It cannot tell merino from lambswool, or cotton from a cotton-modal blend. A longer list mostly buys more confident-but-wrong tags for the user to fix — which is more input, not less.
2. **A field earns its place by changing a decision.** If two materials never alter warmth, formality or weather behaviour, they don't need separate entries. That's why `Acrylic` and `Shearling` are worth adding and `Ramie` isn't.

content.text:
Yes on the second half — and it's better than I implied. But the first half is too strong.

## After #3: degraded, not broken

Three of six terms survive, because `fleece`, `down` and `tweed` are all in the new `MATERIALS` vocabulary. What stops matching is `shearling` and `puffer` (absent from the list — they'd normalise to `"Other"`) and `quilted` (it becomes a *texture*, and the rule only reads material).

So a fleece or a tweed jacket still gets excluded at 30°C. A shearling coat or a quilted puffer stops being caught. Partial regression, and silent — no test fails, because the tests use free-text fixtures.

## After #12: yes, and it's the right mechanism already

Queue #12 doesn't just add texture to scoring — it already models exactly this:

- `textureWarmth(texture): number` — 0..1, `Chunky knit` > `Fine knit`, `Fleece-back` > `Flat`, unknown → `0.5` neutral
- `warmthFit(items, tempC): number` — a target warmth derived from the temperature, so `fine` beats `chunky` at 30° and the reverse at 2°

And its own architecture note says it enters as a **soft preference**: *"the model this codebase has converged on three times (outerwear, colour lean, season)."* So warmth becomes a continuous score against measured temperature, not a keyword list. A chunky merino sweater reads warm; a fine merino tee reads light — same fibre, correctly separated. That's precisely the distinction you raised about weight and weave, and it's already designed.

## The gap between them

#3 is queue 3, #12 is queue 12 — so there's a window of nine plans where the heat rule is quietly worse than it is today. Two ways to close it:

- **Cheap:** while executing #3, add `Shearling` to `MATERIALS` and have the heat rule read `texture` for `Quilted`. Keeps parity until #12 lands.
- **Cleaner:** pull the warmth half of #12 forward and delete `HOT_MATERIALS` entirely when #3 ships, so material-based heat exclusion never exists in a constrained-vocabulary world.

I'd lean cleaner — `HOT_MATERIALS` is a stopgap I only wrote because season stopped guarding heat, and once `texture` exists there's no reason for a keyword list to survive. But that's a call for when you get there, and I've recorded both options in the #3 plan.

One caveat on your framing: even #12 is warmth, not a full weight/weave model. `texture` captures knit structure and surface finish, not fabric weight in gsm. So a tropical wool suit trouser and a flannel one could both be tagged `Flat` and score identically. Better than today by a wide margin, but not the last word.
so a question, when we do a cleaner way, would it work properly after plan 12 or not, as we want

Honestly: **not fully, no.** Two things would still be wrong, and one of them is the same mistake I already made.

## Gap 1 — warmth would read `texture` only, but some warmth lives in `material`

Queue #12 defines `textureWarmth(texture: string | null): number`. Texture alone. Trace the four cases the current rule catches:

| garment | material | texture | reads warm? |
|---|---|---|---|
| fleece | Fleece | Fleece-back | ✓ |
| puffer | Down | Quilted | ✓ |
| shearling coat | *Other* | Pile | ✓ by luck |
| **tweed jacket** | **Tweed** | Twill / Herringbone | **✗** |

Tweed's warmth is in the *fibre and cloth*, not the knit structure — and `Twill` / `Herringbone` are weaves that a linen shirt also uses. So a tweed jacket would score neutral in 32°C heat. Shearling only survives because `Pile` happens to be warm, and its material normalises to `Other`.

That's the same error I made in reverse: I judged warmth from material alone, #12 judges it from texture alone. Neither is sufficient — the signal is `material × texture`, which is exactly the pair your original wool question identified.

## Gap 2 — soft-only doesn't prevent the absurd case

#12 makes warmth a scoring term. A down puffer at 32°C would be *demoted*, not excluded — so with `diversify` tiering the shortlist to 20 candidates, it can still reach the screen on a thin closet. Today it cannot.

There's a real difference between "slightly off-season" — which this project deliberately accepts, better a slightly-off outfit than none — and "physically wrong". A linen shirt tagged `{Winter}` in July is the first. A down jacket at 32°C is the second.

## What would actually work

The project already has the answer, and I under-used it: **the relief rule makes hard filters safe.** `rain → exclude suede` is still hard, and it can no longer empty a required slot. So this isn't soft-versus-hard — it's both, at different severities:

- **`warmth(material, texture)`** as the soft term in scoring — replaces `HOT_MATERIALS` for everything ordinary, and correctly separates a chunky merino sweater from a fine merino tee.
- **A narrow hard exclusion for insulation only** — down, fleece, shearling above roughly 28°C — kept because no weave rescues them, and made safe by the existing relief rule.

So the cleaner path is right, but it needs #12's warmth function widened to take material as well, which is a change to that plan rather than a free consequence of it. Let me record that:

shearling excluded above roughly 28°C, because no weave rescues them. This is safe now in a way it was

- **Substring material matching** — was equality, so `"suede leather"` already slipped past the rain rule.

**⚠️ `HOT_MATERIALS` is a STOPGAP with a planned death date — read before touching warmth.**
Deleting the season filter also deleted the only thing keeping a wool sweater out of a July outfit, so
`weatherRules` gained material exclusions above 25°C. The user (who knows menswear) corrected the first
version, and the correction is the important part: **fibre alone never decides warmth — weight and weave
do.** Tropical, fresco and high-twist wools are summer suiting; merino is worn *for* heat because it
wicks. `items.material` is a bare fibre name, so a "wool" rule cannot tell a summer-weight trouser from a
melton coat, and would bin exactly the smart-casual work wear this app exists to style.

So the list is insulation and coarse heavy weave only — `fleece, shearling, down, quilted, puffer, tweed`
— where no construction makes them summer-appropriate. Wool/merino/cashmere fall through to the
`seasonFit` penalty: demoted, never eliminated. A test pins that a `tropical wool` trouser survives 32°C.

The staged plan, because this is **data-blocked, not deferred by choice**:
1. **Now** — the keyword list. It is all free-text `material` can support.
2. **Queue #3 (`item-data-completeness`)** — creates `items.texture` and constrains `material` to an enum.
   **Do NOT delete the list here**: `fleece`/`down`/`tweed` still match, but `shearling` and `puffer` are
   absent from the new vocabulary and `quilted` becomes a *texture*, so it silently half-breaks. That
   plan now carries a "Vocabulary coverage review" section with the fixes (`TEXTURES` needs an `"Other"`;
   add `Acrylic`, `Shearling`, `Faux leather`, `Modal`).
3. **Queue #12 (`item-signals-in-generator`)** — widen its `textureWarmth(texture)` to
   `warmth(material, texture)` (texture alone misses tweed, whose warmth is in the cloth), keep a narrow
   hard exclusion for insulation (a soft term only demotes, and `diversify` fills 20 slots), **then
   delete `HOT_MATERIALS`.** That plan now carries a "Warmth must read material AND texture" section.

Attempting this before #3 makes things worse, not better: `textureWarmth(null)` is `0.5`, so every
garment would score identically on warmth. **Limit worth stating even after #12:** `texture` records knit
structure, not gsm — a tropical wool and a flannel can both be `Flat`. Nothing in the queue gives weight.

---
name: user-knows-menswear
description: The user has real menswear/textile domain knowledge — check garment assumptions with them rather than encoding folk rules
metadata:
  type: user
---

The user knows clothing properly. On 2026-07-28 they caught a rule I had written that excluded **wool**
from outfits above 25°C, with: *"it depends which type of wool, also his weight, weave."* That was
correct and I was wrong — tropical, fresco and high-twist wools are summer suiting, and merino is worn
*for* heat because it wicks. My substring match was excluding `"merino wool"` outright, which is
backwards.

**Why it matters:** garment rules that sound like common sense ("wool is warm", "linen is summer") are
folk heuristics, and encoding them produces confidently wrong results in exactly the smart-casual
wardrobe Fitcheck is built for. The real determinants are usually weight and construction, which the
data model often does not capture.

**How to apply:** before encoding any rule about how a garment behaves — warmth, formality, weather
suitability, what pairs with what — state the assumption explicitly and check it with them, the way the
wool question resolved. Ask what actually decides the property, then check whether the schema can even
express it; if it cannot, prefer a soft ranking signal over a hard filter rather than guessing. See the
staged `HOT_MATERIALS` plan in [[session-state]].

fine merino tee — the distinction that motivated all of this.

**Keep a narrow hard exclusion for insulation.** A soft term demotes but does not prevent, and
`diversify` fills the shortlist to 20, so a down puffer can still reach the screen at 32°C on a thin
closet. There is a real difference between *slightly off-season* — which this project deliberately
accepts ("better a slightly-off outfit than none") — and *physically wrong*. Keep down / fleece /
shearling excluded above roughly 28°C, because no weave rescues them. This is safe now in a way it was
not before: `eligibleByCategory`'s relief rule guarantees a weather exclusion can narrow a required
slot but never empty it.

**Net result:** delete `HOT_MATERIALS` when this ships, not when queue #3 ships. Between #3 and here it
is degraded but not useless — `fleece`, `down` and `tweed` still match the constrained vocabulary.

**Limit worth stating:** even `warmth(material, texture)` is not a weight model. `texture` captures knit
structure and surface finish, not gsm, so a tropical-weight wool trouser and a flannel one can both be
`Flat` and score identically. Better than a keyword list by a wide margin; not the last word.

**What was actually wrong:** the fixes lived only in sections at the *bottom* of each plan. The task steps still contained the stale code. Anyone executing step-by-step pastes those blocks and never reads the footnote — which is exactly how the seasons plan reverted the coverage fix, twice.

- **DB**: `price numeric` with no `NOT NULL` (it already existed; I only added `texture`)
- **Schema**: `z.number().nonnegative().nullable()` — may be null, and negatives are rejected
- **UI**: placeholder *"Optional — enables cost per wear"*, and an empty box saves as `null`, not `0` — cost-per-wear must never divide by a price the user never gave
- **The tagger never writes it.** `TagSchema` has no `price` field; a photo can't tell you what something cost. It's user-entered only, on item detail

That's also why it's queue #3's job: price here is what makes cost-per-wear possible later (queue #10, wear-stats).

-- Table-level DML grants for `service_role`, the counterpart to
-- 20260721090000_authenticated_grants.sql.

grant select, insert, update, delete on all tables in schema public to service_role;

alter default privileges in schema public
  grant select, insert, update, delete on tables to service_role;

content.text: Both fixed, and verified on device. 305 tests, `tsc` and build clean. **Material / texture / pattern → selects.** Added a `Select` primitive in `ui-fitcheck` rather than inlining, so both edit surfaces stay consistent. On iOS it opens the native wheel, which is a better picker than anything we'd build. Chips stay where they earn their space — category (5) and seasons (4, multi-select). **Colour → collapsible.** It's now a one-line summary showing the swatches and names, expanding to the palette only when you go to change it. It auto-opens when nothing is selected, so it never looks broken. I also had to strengthen the swatch ring: at 20px, `#141414` black on the `#161517` surface read as an empty box. **The image bug was real and worth the diagnosis.** The container computed to 392×**502** when `aspect-[1.3]` should give 392×**301**. The `` was a grid item, so it kept `min-height: auto` — its intrinsic 970×1280 forced the row past the aspect ratio, and Safari let it spill over the fields below. My first fix (`max-h-full`) didn't work either, and the reason is worth recording: a percentage max-height against an **auto-sized grid row** is indefinite, so it resolves to `none`. The fix is absolute positioning — `absolute inset-0 size-full object-contain` — which gives `object-contain` a definite box. Now 392×302 at ratio 1.3 with the image fully inside. Same bug existed on the capture confirm screen; fixed there too. And both now use `.surface-stage` — the radial "lit from above" gradient the design-tokens plan specified for exactly these two screens (`:595` and `:530`) but which I hadn't applied in that PR. **Where the plan stands:** Tasks 1–8 done and committed (vocabulary module, `texture` column, constrained AI schema, both surfaces on shared vocab, colour picker, new fields, persistence, backfill). The backfill normalised 15 legacy materials — your closet now has 8 distinct values, all valid vocabulary. That also needed an unplanned migration: `service_role` had no table grants, so the script hit `42501`. Task 9 is verify-live + PR.
